modules.title: 1 · Building likelihoods
modules.summary: Turn a probability model into an objective for observed data.

stages.title: Building likelihoods: research guide
stages.html:
Building likelihoods

Turn a probability model into an objective for observed data.

A likelihood is the joint density or mass evaluated at the data and viewed as a function of parameters; support and factorization are part of the model.

Workflow. Build the joint density or mass as a function of parameters for observed data.

Diagnostic: Inspect support, independence factorization, and constants. The main failure to avoid is an objective that is not the model's likelihood.

stages.title: Likelihood construction intuition lab
stages.note: Set the true rate and sample size, then watch the Poisson log-likelihood curve tighten around its peak (the MLE = sample mean) as n grows.
stages.template:
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.special import gammaln
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = int({{n}}); lam_true = {{lam}}
x = rng.poisson(lam_true, n)                     # observed counts (support: 0,1,2,...)
mle = x.mean()                                   # Poisson MLE = sample mean
grid = np.linspace(0.2, max(2*lam_true, 2*mle) + 2, 300)
# log-likelihood as a FUNCTION of lambda for the fixed observed data
ll = (x[:, None]*np.log(grid[None, :]) - grid[None, :] - gammaln(x+1)[:, None]).sum(0)
plt.figure(figsize=(6, 3.7))
plt.plot(grid, ll, color="#da9100", lw=2)
plt.axvline(mle, color="#3a7d44", ls="--", lw=1.5, label=f"MLE = {mle:.2f}")
plt.axvline(lam_true, color="#8a8a8a", ls=":", lw=1.5, label=f"true λ = {lam_true:.2f}")
plt.xlabel("λ"); plt.ylabel("log-likelihood  ℓ(λ)")
plt.title("Poisson log-likelihood over the observed counts"); plt.legend()
print(f"MLE (sample mean) = {mle:.3f}   true lambda = {lam_true:.3f}")
print(f"max log-likelihood = {ll.max():.2f}")

stages.title: Building likelihoods: worked Python model
stages.note: Run the reproducible example, then change one assumption and compare the output.
stages.code:
import numpy as np
y = np.array([1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 1])
grid = np.linspace(0.05, 0.95, 181)
loglike = np.array([(y*np.log(p) + (1-y)*np.log(1-p)).sum() for p in grid])
p_hat = grid[np.argmax(loglike)]
print(f"Grid MLE: {p_hat:.3f}")
print(f"Sample mean: {y.mean():.3f}")

modules.title: 2 · Score and information
modules.summary: Use first and second derivatives to characterize estimation and precision.

stages.title: Score and information: research guide
stages.html:
Score and information

Use first and second derivatives to characterize estimation and precision.

The score measures local slope; the information measures curvature and identifies directions in which the data are informative.

Workflow. Differentiate the log-likelihood and interpret zero score at an interior optimum.

Diagnostic: Inspect gradient magnitude and parameter constraints. The main failure to avoid is declaring convergence while the score remains large.

stages.title: Score equations intuition lab
stages.note: Change n and σ and watch the score function: it crosses zero at the MLE, and its slope there IS the information n/σ² that sets the estimate's precision.
stages.template:
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = int({{n}}); sigma = {{sigma}}
x = rng.normal(2.0, sigma, n)                    # Normal, unknown mean mu, known sigma
xbar = x.mean()                                  # MLE of mu = where the score = 0
mu = np.linspace(xbar - 3, xbar + 3, 200)
score = (x[:, None] - mu[None, :]).sum(0) / sigma**2   # d/dmu of log-likelihood
info = n / sigma**2                              # Fisher information = -slope of score
plt.figure(figsize=(6, 3.7))
plt.plot(mu, score, color="#1f6feb", lw=2, label="score S(μ)")
plt.axhline(0, color="#8a8a8a", lw=1)
plt.axvline(xbar, color="#3a7d44", ls="--", lw=1.5, label=f"MLE = {xbar:.2f}")
plt.xlabel("μ"); plt.ylabel("score  S(μ)")
plt.title(f"Information I = n/σ² = {info:.1f}  (steeper = more informative)")
plt.legend()
print(f"Fisher information I(mu) = {info:.2f}")
print(f"asymptotic SE = sqrt(1/I) = {np.sqrt(1/info):.4f}")

modules.title: 3 · Identification and profile likelihood
modules.summary: Detect observationally equivalent parameters before trusting optimization.

stages.title: Identification and profile likelihood: research guide
stages.html:
Identification and profile likelihood

Detect observationally equivalent parameters before trusting optimization.

Numerical convergence cannot repair identification: a flat profile or rank-deficient Hessian signals that the data do not separate parameters.

Workflow. Use expected or observed curvature to quantify local precision.

Diagnostic: Inspect Hessian sign, conditioning, and information equality. The main failure to avoid is standard errors from a flat or wrongly signed objective.

stages.title: Information and curvature intuition lab
stages.note: Push the regressor correlation ρ toward 1: the profile log-likelihood ridge for β₁ goes flat and the X'X condition number and SE explode — the data can't separate the two effects.
stages.template:
import numpy as np, statsmodels.api as sm, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = int({{n}}); rho = {{rho}}
x1 = rng.normal(0, 1, n)
x2 = rho*x1 + np.sqrt(1 - rho**2)*rng.normal(0, 1, n)   # correlated regressor
y = 1.0*x1 + 1.0*x2 + rng.normal(0, 1, n)               # true betas both = 1
X = np.column_stack([np.ones(n), x1, x2])
res = sm.OLS(y, X).fit()
se1 = res.bse[1]; cond = np.linalg.cond(X.T @ X)
# profile log-likelihood over beta1, concentrating out const, beta2, sigma
Z = np.column_stack([np.ones(n), x2]); Zp = np.linalg.pinv(Z)
b1 = np.linspace(1 - 3, 1 + 3, 150); prof = []
for b in b1:
    r = y - b*x1
    resid = r - Z @ (Zp @ r)
    s2 = np.mean(resid**2)
    prof.append(-0.5*n*(np.log(2*np.pi*s2) + 1))
plt.figure(figsize=(6, 3.7))
plt.plot(b1, prof, color="#b5179e", lw=2)
plt.axvline(1.0, color="#8a8a8a", ls=":", lw=1.5, label="true β₁ = 1")
plt.xlabel("β₁"); plt.ylabel("profile log-likelihood")
plt.title(f"cond(X'X) = {cond:,.0f}   SE(β̂₁) = {se1:.2f}"); plt.legend()
print(f"condition number of X'X = {cond:,.0f}")
print(f"SE of beta1 = {se1:.3f}  (flat profile => weak identification)")

modules.title: 4 · Numerical optimization
modules.summary: Scale, initialize, constrain, and verify nonlinear estimators.

stages.title: Numerical optimization: research guide
stages.html:
Numerical optimization

Scale, initialize, constrain, and verify nonlinear estimators.

A credible optimum survives alternative starting values and has a small gradient, admissible parameters, and sensible curvature.

Workflow. Scale parameters, use defensible starts, and verify more than one convergence signal.

Diagnostic: Inspect gradient, Hessian, bounds, and sensitivity to starts. The main failure to avoid is a local or boundary solution reported as a unique optimum.

stages.title: Numerical optimization intuition lab
stages.note: The mixture negative log-likelihood is symmetric with two minima; slide the optimizer's start across the local maximum at 0 and watch it converge to a different solution.
stages.template:
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.optimize import minimize
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
sep = {{sep}}; x0 = {{x0}}
z = rng.random(300) < 0.5
data = np.where(z, rng.normal(sep, 1, 300), rng.normal(-sep, 1, 300))
def nll(mu):
    m = np.atleast_1d(mu)[0]
    dens = 0.5*np.exp(-0.5*(data - m)**2) + 0.5*np.exp(-0.5*(data + m)**2)
    return -np.sum(np.log(dens + 1e-12))
grid = np.linspace(-sep - 3, sep + 3, 400)
curve = np.array([nll(m) for m in grid])
opt = minimize(nll, x0, method="Nelder-Mead")
mstar = opt.x[0]
grad = (nll(mstar + 1e-4) - nll(mstar - 1e-4)) / 2e-4
plt.figure(figsize=(6, 3.7))
plt.plot(grid, curve, color="#d1495b", lw=2)
plt.axvline(x0, color="#8a8a8a", ls=":", lw=1.5, label=f"start = {x0:.1f}")
plt.axvline(mstar, color="#3a7d44", ls="--", lw=1.5, label=f"converged μ = {mstar:.2f}")
plt.xlabel("μ"); plt.ylabel("negative log-likelihood")
plt.title("Multimodal objective: the start decides the basin"); plt.legend()
print(f"start = {x0:.2f}  ->  converged mu = {mstar:.3f}")
print(f"gradient at solution = {grad:.2e}  (small => a local optimum, not necessarily unique)")

modules.title: 5 · Robust inference and model comparison
modules.summary: Match covariance estimators and comparison tools to the maintained model.

stages.title: Robust inference and model comparison: research guide
stages.html:
Robust inference and model comparison

Match covariance estimators and comparison tools to the maintained model.

Model-based information, sandwich uncertainty, likelihood-ratio tests, and information criteria answer different questions.

Workflow. Use sandwich uncertainty under misspecification while stating the pseudo-true target.

Diagnostic: Inspect score covariance versus Hessian curvature. The main failure to avoid is model-based precision that assumes a false conditional variance.

stages.title: Robust likelihood inference intuition lab
stages.note: Turn up the heteroskedasticity γ: at γ=0 the classical and sandwich (HC3) standard errors agree, but as the conditional variance bends they diverge — only the sandwich estimator tracks the truth.
stages.template:
import numpy as np, statsmodels.api as sm, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = int({{n}}); g = {{gamma}}
x = rng.normal(0, 1, n)
sd = np.exp(g*x)                                  # variance depends on x => heteroskedastic
y = 1 + 2*x + sd*rng.normal(0, 1, n)              # true slope = 2
res = sm.OLS(y, sm.add_constant(x)).fit()
se_model = res.bse[1]                             # model-based (assumes homoskedasticity)
se_sand = float(res.HC3_se[1])                    # sandwich / robust SE
plt.figure(figsize=(6, 3.7))
bars = plt.bar(["model-based", "sandwich (HC3)"], [se_model, se_sand],
               color=["#8a8a8a", "#1f6feb"])
for b, v in zip(bars, [se_model, se_sand]):
    plt.text(b.get_x() + b.get_width()/2, v, f"{v:.3f}", ha="center", va="bottom")
plt.ylabel("SE of slope β̂₁")
plt.title(f"γ = {g:.1f}:  robust / model-based ratio = {se_sand/se_model:.2f}")
print(f"model-based SE = {se_model:.4f}   sandwich SE = {se_sand:.4f}")
print(f"ratio (=1 only under homoskedasticity) = {se_sand/se_model:.3f}")
